Split view is in, driven in the browser on two different questions.

**What the room now sees.** A catalog strip sits above both panes — `kpi · bar · line · table` — with the kinds the current spec used lit in cyan and the rest recessed, plus the plain statement *"the model may only use these four."* Ask "fastest-growing roles" and `kpi` + `table` light up; ask "junior dev jobs" and it's `kpi` + `bar`. The JSON no longer vanishes at the moment of payoff; both halves stay on screen together, which is the whole point of the demo.

**Two fixes after looking at the first render**, neither visible in the diff:

The numerals came free: `BeatFooter` already switches from ticks to numerals at six beats or fewer (`NUMERAL_LIMIT`), so two beats get exactly Era 1's treatment — filled numeral for live, label crossfading in a reserved slot beneath. No change to the footer was needed.

**One structural change to make it possible.** `Era4Runtime` was rendering `CompanyBrain` internally, so the two halves couldn't be gated separately. `CompanyBrain` now sits in `masterclass.tsx` in its own `BeatSlot`, which is how every Era 3 demo already works — one component per beat, gated at the call site.

Stepping back keeps both demos on screen, since `useBeats` gates on `furthest` rather than `current` — you can re-explain the dashboard without the ambient figure vanishing mid-sentence.

**I added a test** (`142 pass` now, up from 141). The gating depends on the string ids in `beats.ts` matching the `has("compiled")` / `has("ambient")` calls in `masterclass.tsx` — a rename on one side would silently hide a demo for the entire talk, and nothing in the suite would have noticed. export interface LadderStage {
  artifact: "diff" | "plan" | "design";
  /** the artifact's rendered lines (mono) */
  body: readonly string[];
  line: string;
  read: string;
  year: "2024" | "2025" | "2026";
}

export const LADDER_STAGES: readonly LadderStage[] = [
  {
    artifact: "diff",
    body: [
      "+ import { validateDiscount } from './validation';",
      "+",
      "+ export function applyDiscount(cart, code) {",
      "+   const result = validateDiscount(code);",
      "+   if (!result.valid) {",
      "+     return { ...cart, discount: 0, warning: result.reason };",
      "+   }",
      "+   return { ...cart, discount: result.amount };",
      "+ }",
      "- export function applyDiscount(cart, code) {",
      "-   return { ...cart, discount: DISCOUNTS[code] };",
      "- }",
      "+ export function validateDiscount(code) {",
      "+   if (typeof code !== 'string' || code.length === 0) {",

content.thinking:
I see the issue now—those three pill toggles look like filter options rather than showing a visual hierarchy. The real concept here is a descending ladder where the artifact shrinks each year, moving from code down to plan down to design, but the current layout doesn't communicate that progression at all.

I'm exploring two main directions: either stacking the rungs vertically as an accordion where each rung expands to reveal its artifact, making the descent literal and the shrinking text visible as you move down—or displaying all three side by side so the wall of diff versus the short plan versus three lines of design creates the visual argument about shrinkage. The challenge is balancing that with presenter mode, which needs to gate it as one beat at a time.

The stronger move is reusing the codebase's existing tab grammar: the three years become folder tabs on a recessed band that merges into the artifact panel below, keeping the established idiom. The "what I read" becomes the panel's header line, and I add a quantitative shrink indicator—line counts like "27 lines" → "5 steps" → "3 sentences"—to make the descent measurable and reinforce the ladder metaphor. The key insight is adding a visual "reading load" bar beneath the header that shrinks proportionally across the three tabs—showing 27/27, then 5/27, then 3/27 of the full width. That single element makes the compression argument instantly clear without needing extra explanation. I'll need to track a `volume` metric for each stage to drive that visualization. So I'll measure everything in lines read: 241 for the diff, 5 for the plan, 3 for the design. That's consistent and honest. A linear bar will be dramatic—the full width for 241, then tiny slivers for the others—and I can display the numbers prominently to make the comparison clear. I'm designing the header with "I read the code" on the left and "241 lines read" on the right in monospace, with the bar underneath. Now I need to fix the tense so 2024 and 2025 read as clearly past. "Proofread" works perfectly for 2024 since it echoes the literature degree reference and clearly signals past tense. For 2025, "checked the plan" is cleaner than "approved" or "signed off." I'm settling on Option Set A as the strongest choice: proofread for 2024, checked for 2025, and keeping the present tense for 2026.

The tab structure should show only years, with the action lines moving into the panel headers—that solves the visual clutter issue. Now I'm deciding whether to present this plan to the user or just build it directly.

Given the pattern from before where he asked me to apply design skills and I built it successfully, I'll build the UI with my recommended copy option and present the alternatives as swappable. That keeps momentum going while still giving him the choice. I need to update the stages data to include line counts and adjust the read strings, then restructure the component layout.

content.thinking:
I'm setting up the tab styling with a semi-transparent foreground background and dark mode variant, where the active tab uses a muted background that seamlessly connects with the panel below. Now I'm building out the main content structure as a rounded container with a subtle border.

Building the reading tracker panel... Calculating the bar widths with those line counts produces tiny slivers, so I'm adding a minimum width of 3 pixels to keep them visible, and using cyan as the accent color since it's the signature of the design. The bar itself represents the reading load meaningfully even at small percentages.

For the copy, I'm setting the line counts to 241 for 2024 (the full diff), 5 for 2025 (the plan steps), and 3 for 2026 (the design sentences), with labels that reflect what was actually read in each year.

I'm realizing the "read" verb creates a pronunciation trap—"proofread" past tense sounds like "proof-red," which mirrors the read/red ambiguity I'm trying to avoid. I need to sidestep any compound with "read" entirely. Better options are "checked every line myself" for 2024, "reviewed the plan instead" for 2025, and keeping "I read the design. Tests read the code." for 2026 since those are simple present tense without the homophone problem.

But all sentences might be cleaner and more consistent: "I checked every line," "I reviewed the plan," and "I read the design. Tests read the code." That's unambiguous and avoids any tense traps.

I'll go with the sentence version and offer the noun-phrase set as an alternative. content.text:
The ladder is one object now, verified across all three years.

**Structure.** Three pills and a floating result became a single bordered panel: folder tabs showing only the year, the live one carrying the panel's fill so it merges downward — the same grammar Era 1's `prompt-tabs` and Era 2's editor already speak, rather than a fourth idiom. Inside it: a header row (*what* I read, left; *how much*, right), the reading-load bar, the artifact, and the verdict behind a top rule. Nothing floats.

**The bar is the argument.** 241 lines of diff → ~120 → 3, on one honest unit. Full width, then half, then a sliver you can barely see at 2026 — which is the demo's whole claim, made as a measurement instead of a sentence. Your correction is in: 2025 counts everything under the five headlines, not the headlines, and renders as `~120` with an `approx` flag so an estimate never masquerades as a tally.

**Tense.** `I checked every line.` (2024) · `I reviewed the plan.` (2025) · `I read the design. Tests read the code.` (2026) — "read" now appears only where it's genuinely present tense, and the two past years use verbs that can't be misread.

**Two things I found while in there:**

- **The diff had lost its indentation.** These are `div`s, so HTML was collapsing the leading spaces and every nested line sat flush against the `+`. Pre-existing, and the other demos avoid it with `whitespace-pre` — their comments literally call it "load-bearing." Now fixed here too.
- **I broke the file mid-way and fixed it.** I put a JSX comment inside `cond && ( … )`, which isn't valid, and the formatter then mangled the closing tags into a syntax error. Caught by typecheck, repaired, re-verified.

Lint on this file is now **3 findings, down from 4** at the committed baseline — extracting `diffTone` retired a nested ternary. 142 tests pass, typecheck clean, no console errors.

Two files modified and uncommitted: `era3-ladder/index.tsx`, `era3-ladder/stages.ts`.

One thing I deliberately didn't touch: the 2025 artifact still displays only the five headlines, while the metric now counts the detail beneath them. If that gap bothers you on screen, the fix is to show a step expanded with its detail — say the word and I'll do it.

content.text:
The harness now moves when you run it, driven end-to-end in the browser and compared before/after.

**Every diff row owns a property of the skeleton.** Previously only `padding` was wired, so five of six findings struck themselves off a list while the mockups sat still. Now each resolution visibly pulls the candidate toward the target, in step with its log line:

| Diff | What moves |
|---|---|
| padding-top 48→32 | gap under the heading closes |
| font-weight 600→500 | heading bar thins |
| heading width −16px | heading bar widens to match |
| heading color ΔE 4.2 | heading bar lightens |
| button width 120→108 | CTA narrows |

**I also fixed a correctness bug I found while wiring it.** The target was rendering `tight={false}` and the converged candidate `tight={true}` — so a "matching" run left the two panels visibly *different*. The target now renders as if every diff were fixed, because it's the thing being matched; a clean run genuinely makes the panels identical.

**The exception is now visible rather than only textual.** The excepted embed renders as an amber dashed block on the candidate against a neutral one on the target, and it stays amber after the count hits zero — which is what earns the closing line about judgment. Renamed to **social embed** everywhere: the mockups, the diff row, the log line, and the verdict (`The embed stays flagged`), plus a test name. No `stripe` anywhere in the demo.

**Controls.** Validate is gone completely — not just the button but the `validate` action and the `validated` state field, so no dead reducer branch is left behind; its two tests were replaced with one that pins the behaviour that actually matters (the excepted diff survives a full run — clear ≠ identical). Reset moved out of the terminal to below the demo as a ghost `Button`, matching Era 3's other demos, and it's disabled while a run is in progress.

Verified: run → count `5`→`0`, log fills, candidate converges, `▸ match` appears; Reset → back to `5` with the marker cleared. 142 tests pass, typecheck clean, zero console errors.

I'm noting some ambiguities to clarify: whether the timer stops when transitioning out of execute, what the button labels should be at each stage, and what the attention hint displays.

The deeper insight is that this shifts the demo's message: instead of "the machine handles most of the work and you only gate one column," it becomes "you're making a deliberate choice at every transition point," which makes the final observation about where the clicks went—and therefore where the actual work happened—much more powerful. Each lane requires three human decisions across the three lanes, making the presenter's agency explicit throughout.

I need to figure out the exact button labels and messaging at each transition, especially between execute and validation, since the semantics matter for how the workflow feels. I'm also thinking through the timer behavior—it should measure just the execute phase and stop when moving to validation, then hold that elapsed time. The five-minute cap stays hidden as a safety limit. And I should verify whether the three lanes keep their distinct metadata from the original design, then update the reducer tests to match the new state machine.

Given how much is in play here—state management, timers, tests, and UI—the best approach is to nail down those 2-3 open decisions first, then build it out cleanly rather than guessing and refactoring later.

I'm recognizing this is a major architectural shift—moving from auto-advancing behavior to click-driven progression with timers—and all the existing tests are built around the old model. Before I start refactoring, I should lock in the design since it's the most substantial change we've discussed, especially given how the state labels define what the demo communicates. The key is establishing a symmetric state machine across all three lanes that flows from planned through execution with timer logic, then transitions based on user interaction. The tense descriptions still hold because they capture when the planning happened, not the demo's current state — worth noting that distinction. The verdict line needs updating since every boundary now requires a click, so something like "Your clicks are all at the edges. The middle is the agent's" works better, and the done-state message about noticing where clicks went still lands. All three lanes start in planned state, so the presenter hands them off sequentially to show the parallelism. For reduced motion, the timer just stops animating rather than fast-forwarding since the flow is now click-driven.

I need to nail down the button labels for the two later transitions and confirm whether the timer freezes at validation or keeps running through it. The nine-click flow does make the demo longer to drive live, but that's intentional — the whole point is letting the user control when each handoff happens. I'll put together a compact design with my recommended labels and flag the two assumptions, then ask for approval before building.

For the transitions, I'm settling on `Hand off →` for the plan cell, `Validate →` to move into validation, and `Accept ✓` to mark it validated. The final state would show `VALIDATED ✓` to match what's already in use.

The spec is clear on the semantics—whether lanes auto-advance, how handoffs work—so the main risk is just getting the labels right, which is easy to adjust. I'll build it with these labels flagged as swappable and state my assumptions upfront so he can tweak them in a line if needed.

Now I'm setting up the reducer with the core types: lanes can be in planned, executing, validating, or validated states, and each tracks elapsed time. The actions handle transitions between phases—handoff moves a lane from planned to executing, validation moves it to validating, accept finalizes it—plus a tick action for time tracking and reset to start over. There's also a five-minute execution cap to keep things bounded.

I'm adding helper functions to check if any lane is actively running (which drives the animation interval), whether the board is completely done, and a formatter for displaying elapsed time in a readable mono format. The UI will show three cells per lane with buttons and live status indicators. I'm settling on putting the "Start validation →" button in the validate cell itself—clicking there naturally pulls the lane forward. The execute cell will show just the timer while running, keeping each column to a single control. Once validation starts, that same cell switches to show the "Accept ✓" button, maintaining a clean left-to-right flow.

During execution, both the timer and the validation button will be visible, which actually signals "work in progress, here's your next action"—that feels right. I'll highlight whichever cell has the actionable button to draw attention there.

Actually, I could simplify this: instead of using a ring to target specific cells, I'll just give every actionable button the same solid styling (foreground background with inverted text), which already makes it pop. That's cleaner than managing multiple attention states.

The subtitle needs updating too—it currently says the board runs itself, but that's not true anymore. It should be "Three real streams from my board. Every lane runs plan → execute → validate — and every move between them is yours."

For the verdict messages: keep "Notice where your clicks went. That's where the job went" when done, and add "Hand one off, then the next. The agent works while you decide" before completion.

Now I'm writing out the core files—the reducer with its logic, tests, the main component, and the lane definitions. I'll also set up a timer that ticks every second while any lane is executing, dispatching tick events to track elapsed time.

content.text:
Read the whole pipeline. This is a real state-machine change — lanes currently auto-advance on ticks with two hardcoded gates, and all 11 reducer tests describe that behaviour. Here's what I'm building, with my assumptions marked so you can correct them cheaply:

- **All three lanes start in `plan`.** Each needs its own hand-off, so you can start one and hand off the next two while the first grinds.
- **Nothing auto-advances.** `execute` runs until *you* move it; the hidden cap just stops the clock at 5:00.
- **Three clicks per lane:** `Hand off →` (plan) · `Validate →` (send the agent's work to validation) · `Accept ✓` (validated).
- **The timer freezes when the lane leaves `execute`** and keeps showing what the run took — "the time it took", as you put it.

content.text:
The board now works the way you described it. Screenshot above is mid-run: one lane accepted, one executing at 0:23, one still waiting for its hand-off.

**The state machine is entirely click-driven.** All three lanes start in `plan`; nothing crosses a column unless you move it. Three clicks per lane — `Hand off →`, `Validate →`, `Accept ✓` — nine in total, and the previous auto-advancing ticks, the two hardcoded gates (`rag`'s hand-off, `deps`'s merge approval) and `attentionTarget` are gone.

**Each lane carries its own clock.** It starts at hand-off, ticks while the agent works, and freezes the moment the lane leaves `execute` — so the cell shows `⏱ 0:23` running, then `✓ 0:23` as the record of what the run took. The hidden 5-minute cap stops the number growing without moving the lane; it sits there waiting for you either way.

Driven in the browser, not just unit-tested: handed off `rag`, waited, handed off `wp` while the first was still running → two independent clocks reading `0:05` and `0:03`, exactly the 2s stagger between my clicks, and `2 in flight`. Then `Validate →` froze `rag` at `0:15` and swapped the cell to `Accept ✓`; `Accept ✓` produced `VALIDATED ✓` and dropped the counter to `1 in flight`.

**The copy now says what you said.** The old subtitle claimed *"The board runs itself — click where it asks you"* and the verdict claimed *"Only one column ever needs you"* — both false under this model, and both understating the point:

> Three real streams from my board. Nothing crosses a column unless I move it, so all three sit in my head at once. Three is roughly my ceiling — not the agent's.

> *Hand one off, then the next. The lanes run in parallel; attention doesn't.*
> — and once all three are accepted —
> *Nine decisions across three lanes. The limit was never what the agent could carry — it was how much I could hold at once.*

I also added a quiet **`n in flight`** counter beside the reset. It's the number the argument rests on: it climbs as you fan out and is the thing you're actually holding in your head. Cut it if it's noise.

Eleven reducer tests replaced with eleven new ones covering the new machine — parallel clocks, the freeze, the cap, out-of-order transitions refused, a second hand-off not restarting a running lane. 142 tests pass, typecheck clean, zero console errors, no new lint findings.

content.text:
Rewritten in your register — short declaratives, the plain admission, the two-beat ending. Walked the full nine clicks to confirm every string lands:

> **Three lanes, one head**
> Three real streams from my board. Nothing moves between columns unless I move it, so I hold all three at once — and that is the tiring part. The agent could take a fourth. I couldn't.

> *Hand one off, then the next. The work runs in parallel. My attention doesn't.*
> — after all nine clicks —
> *Nine decisions, three lanes. None of them was hard. Holding all three at once was.*

Four decisions in that rewrite:

- **The headline changed to "one head."** "One week" measured the work; the demo isn't about the work, it's about you. It also matches the deck's own cadence — *Seven years, three machines* → *Three lanes, one head*.
- **The counter reads `3 in my head`, not `3 in flight`.** "In flight" is ops jargon that quietly credits the system; "in my head" names who's actually carrying it, and it climbs to 3 as you fan out and drains to 0 as you accept. Verified both ends.
- **"Ceiling" is gone.** *"The agent could take a fourth. I couldn't."* says the same thing without the abstraction, and lands on the admission — the move you use in Era 1 with the literature degree.
- **The closing line concedes before it claims.** *"None of them was hard. Holding all three at once was."* That's your point from the message: the tax isn't difficulty, it's simultaneity.

142 tests pass, typecheck clean, zero console errors.

Three files uncommitted for this demo: `era3-pipeline/index.tsx`, `reducer.ts`, `reducer.test.ts`.

One thing I left alone but would flag: `lanes.ts` still tags the lanes *"present — you plan this one" / "past — you already planned it" / "permanent — planned once, runs weekly."* Those were written when only one lane needed planning. Now you hand off all three yourself, so "you already planned it" sits oddly next to a `Hand off →` button you're about to press. Want me to rework those three lines too?

content.thinking:
I'm thinking about headline options that follow the pattern of "Three features, one attention" — using concrete units of work paired with a scarce resource. Looking at the existing headlines in the deck like "Three lanes, one week" and "Seven years, three machines," I'm generating variations that maintain this structure and rhythm.

The core options range from his original sketch "Three features, one attention" (which has an interesting grammatical oddness since attention is uncountable) to more conventional phrasings like "Three features, one attention span" that feel clearer but more clinical. There's also the personal punch of "Three features, one me," the bodily specificity of "Three features, one pair of eyes," and the clever engineering reference in "Three features, one thread of attention" — where "thread" works both as a metaphor for thought and as a nod to concurrency that the technical audience will catch. I'm also considering "Three features, one working memory" since that's cognitively precise and connects to Eric's background.

Given his cognitive science and M.Ed. training, "working memory" feels like the strongest choice — it names the exact mechanism he described (the limit of what he can hold in mind without exhaustion) and would resonate with his expertise, though I should check whether it reads as jargon to a mixed audience. The alternative is sticking with "attention span" for punchiness and clarity. I should offer a few solid options with a clear recommendation, and also flag that the closing line says "Twelve decisions across three things" — swapping "things" for "features" would tighten the consistency.

content.text:
Four, all in that direction:

**A — `Three features, one attention span`**
The plainest true version. "Attention span" is the everyday name for exactly the thing that runs out, and it needs no explaining from the stage. Slightly clinical, and it's the phrase a productivity blog would reach for.

**B — `Three features, one working memory`**
Names the actual mechanism rather than the symptom — holding three independent contexts *is* a working-memory load, and that's why it's tiring rather than merely busy. Given your background this is the most precise option, and precision here is a small credibility signal to anyone in the room who knows the term. Risk: one beat of jargon.

**C — `Three features, one me`**
The punchiest and the most human — it lands the joke and the limit in three words. Reads well on a projector. Risk: it's the least specific about *why* three is the ceiling, so the subtitle has to do all the work.

**D — `Three features, one thread of attention`**
"Thread" quietly does double duty: three jobs running concurrently against a single thread. Engineers get the pun; everyone else reads "train of thought" and loses nothing. Longest of the four.

**I'd take B.** The demo's whole argument is that the bottleneck moved from the machine to you, and "working memory" is the only one of these that names the bottleneck instead of gesturing at it — it turns a complaint about being busy into a claim about capacity, which is the more interesting thing you're actually saying. C is my second choice if you want the room to laugh rather than nod.

One note on your sketch: **"one attention"** on its own reads as a grammar slip on a slide, since attention isn't countable — the eye trips before the meaning lands. All four above keep your direction while giving the noun something to attach to.

Whichever you pick, I'd make the closing line agree with it: *"Twelve decisions across three things"* → *"across three features"*.

feat(web): rebuild the board demo around attention, not throughput

The board used to run itself: lanes advanced on a timer with two hardcoded
gates, which argued that the machine does the work and you approve it. That
is not what the week actually feels like. Every transition is now a click,
so the demo shows the real constraint — how many independent things one
person can hold at once.

Board
- All three features start unplanned; each needs its own hand-off, so you
  fan out and then carry all three.
- Nothing advances on its own. Four clicks a feature: hand off, done,
  validate, accept.
- `done` only stops the clock and `toValidation` only moves the work. They
  were one button, which conflated the agent finishing with me deciding the
  result was worth validating. Splitting them also leaves exactly one live
  action per row, which matters when driving this from a stage.
- Each feature carries its own clock, frozen when it leaves execute. A
  hidden five-minute cap keeps a forgotten run from counting into the hours
  without moving the feature.
- The counter reads "n in my head" rather than "in flight": a stopped clock
  still counts, because a finished run nobody has looked at is still mine.

Copy
- "Three lanes, one week" measured the work; the demo is about the person.
  Now "Three features, one thread of attention", and no lanes, streams,
  columns or parallel anywhere on screen.
- The old lines claimed "the board runs itself" and "only one column ever
  needs you". Both were false under this model and both undersold the point.

Meter
- One subscription, not two.
- The aside is "how I work" with no date: it describes a standing practice,
  so a date would only imply it goes stale. FieldNote's date is now optional,
  rendered as one expression so an absent date cannot leave a dangling
  separator behind.

143 tests pass; typecheck clean.
